title: Chapter 4 — The Counterpane
paragraphs: Waking next morning around daylight, I found Queequeg's arm thrown over me in the most loving and affectionate manner. You'd have thought I was his wife. The bedspread was patchwork, full of odd little multicolored squares and triangles; and his arm, tattooed all over with an endless Cretan labyrinth of patterns — no two parts exactly the same shade, probably from keeping his arm at sea in random patches of sun and shade, his sleeves rolled up unevenly at different times — this arm, I say, looked exactly like a strip of that same patchwork quilt. Lying partly on the quilt as it was when I first woke, I could barely tell arm from bedspread, they blended their colors so perfectly. Only the sense of weight and pressure told me Queequeg was hugging me.

My feelings were strange. Let me try to explain. When I was a child, something very similar happened to me — whether it was real or a dream, I could never decide. Here's what happened. I'd been getting into some kind of mischief — trying to crawl up the chimney, I think, having seen a little chimney sweep do it a few days before. My stepmother, who was always either whipping me or sending me to bed without supper, dragged me out by my legs and packed me off to bed, though it was only two in the afternoon on June 21st — the longest day of the year. I felt miserable. But there was nothing to be done, so up I went to my little room on the third floor, undressed as slowly as possible to kill time, and with a bitter sigh crawled between the sheets.

I lay there miserably calculating that sixteen full hours had to pass before I could hope for freedom. Sixteen hours in bed! My back ached just thinking about it. And it was so bright out — sunshine pouring through the window, coaches rattling in the streets, cheerful voices throughout the house. I felt worse and worse. Finally I got up, dressed, and tiptoed downstairs in my stockings to find my stepmother. I threw myself at her feet and begged her, as a special favor, to give me a good spanking for my misbehavior — anything rather than condemning me to that unbearable time in bed. But she was the most conscientious of stepmothers, and back I went to my room. For several hours I lay wide awake, feeling worse than I've ever felt since, even in my greatest misfortunes. At last I must have fallen into a troubled doze, and slowly waking from it — half-steeped in dreams — I opened my eyes. The room, which had been sunlit before, was now wrapped in total darkness. Instantly a shock ran through me. Nothing could be seen, nothing heard — but a supernatural hand seemed to be placed in mine. My arm hung over the bedspread, and the nameless, unimaginable, silent form to which the hand belonged seemed seated right beside my bed. For what felt like ages upon ages, I lay there frozen with the most terrible fear, not daring to pull my hand away, yet thinking that if I could just move it one inch, the horrible spell would break. I don't know how this sensation finally faded. But waking in the morning, I remembered it all with a shudder, and for days and weeks and months afterward I lost myself in futile attempts to explain the mystery. Even now, I still puzzle over it.

Now, take away the awful fear, and my feelings at sensing that supernatural hand were very similar to what I experienced waking up to find Queequeg's tattooed arm around me. But gradually the events of last night came back, one by one, in solid reality, and I realized the comedy of my situation. I tried to move his arm — to unlock his bridegroom's embrace — but he hugged me tight in his sleep, as if nothing but death could part us. I tried to wake him: 'Queequeg!' — but his only answer was a snore. I rolled over, my neck feeling like it was in a horse collar, and suddenly felt a scratch. Throwing back the bedspread, there lay the tomahawk, sleeping by the savage's side like a hatchet-faced baby. Fine situation, I thought — in bed in a strange house in broad daylight, with a cannibal and a tomahawk! 'Queequeg! In the name of goodness, Queequeg, wake up!' After much wriggling and loud protests about the impropriety of one man hugging another in such a matrimonial fashion, I managed to extract a grunt. He drew back his arm, shook himself all over like a Newfoundland dog fresh from the water, and sat up stiff as a board, looking at me and rubbing his eyes as if he didn't quite remember how I came to be there — though a dim awareness of knowing me seemed to be slowly dawning. Meanwhile I lay quietly studying him, no longer seriously worried, determined to observe this curious creature closely. When his mind was finally made up about me, he jumped out of bed and through signs and gestures let me know that, if I wished, he would dress first and then leave the entire room to me. Very civilized of you, Queequeg, I thought. The truth is, these so-called savages have an innate sense of courtesy, say what you will. I pay Queequeg this particular compliment because he treated me with such kindness, while I was guilty of great rudeness — staring at him from bed and watching his every move, my curiosity getting the better of my manners. But a man like Queequeg you don't see every day.

He began dressing from the top down — first putting on his very tall beaver hat, and then, still without trousers, hunting for his boots. What on earth he was doing, I can't say, but his next move was to cram himself — boots in hand, hat on head — under the bed. From various violent gaspings and strainings, I gathered he was battling to get his boots on, though no rule of propriety I've ever heard of requires a man to be private while putting on boots. Queequeg, you see, was a creature in transition — neither caterpillar nor butterfly. He was just civilized enough to display his oddness in the strangest ways. His education wasn't yet complete; he was still an undergraduate. If he'd been less civilized, he probably wouldn't have bothered with boots at all. But if he'd been less savage, he'd never have dreamed of getting under the bed to put them on. He finally emerged with his hat badly dented over his eyes, creaking and limping around the room — those damp, wrinkled cowhide boots clearly pinching him on this bitter cold morning.

Seeing that there were no curtains on the window, and that the narrow street gave the neighbors a clear view into the room, and noticing what an indecent figure Queequeg made in nothing but his hat and boots, I begged him to speed up and especially to get into his trousers as soon as possible. He complied, then proceeded to wash himself. Any Christian at that hour would have washed his face, but Queequeg, to my amazement, restricted his washing to his chest, arms, and hands. He then put on his vest, picked up a piece of hard soap from the washstand, lathered his face, and — I was watching for his razor when, lo and behold, he grabbed the harpoon from the bed corner, slid off the wooden shaft, unsheathed the head, honed it a little on his boot, and striding to the mirror on the wall, began vigorously scraping — or rather harpooning — his cheeks. Using the finest cutlery with a vengeance, I thought. Later, I was less surprised when I learned how fine the steel of a harpoon head is, and how razor-sharp the edges are always kept.
The rest of his grooming was quickly finished, and he marched proudly out of the room wrapped in his great pilot jacket, carrying his harpoon like a marshal's baton.
